transcript:
00:00:00 - Sam Turner: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh I'm Sam from Redwood, I'll hand it to Priya for the deep dive but quick agenda, p95/p99, streaming, kv cache, batching, quantize stuff, and then Q&A, sound good?
00:00:12 - Alex Kim: yeah that works, thanks Sam, we've got Maya, Jordan and Rita on the call, we're particularly worried about p99 spikes during peak teleop sessions, so curious how you handle that with dedicated infra vs hosted.
00:00:30 - Priya Shah: cool, quick context, Redwood's runtime does continuous batching and kv caching; for streaming we flush tokens as soon as they're available which helps latency for interactive sessions, non-streaming we wait for full response which can reduce CPU overhead but adds tail. bear with me while I share a slide - (screen)
00:00:50 - Jordan Price: earlier we saw a p99 1.8s spike when network retry hit, is that something you can tune?
00:01:02 - Priya Shah: yes, network retries and extra hop—especially in VPC peering or cross-region calls—are a common source; we usually recommend colocating the model endpoint in same region and enabling TCP keepalive, but more importantly, design for fallbacks: lower-quality quantized variant or cached stub during degradation.
00:01:25 - Maya Lopez: question, when kv cache is cold, how bad is the hit for a 2k prompt?
00:01:33 - Priya Shah: cold-cache for long sequences can add 10-30% extra latency depending on architecture—because you miss prefix reuse and must re-run key generation; in practice p95 holds but p99 moves. For a 2k prompt on a 80B model we saw cold-cache p99 jump from ~720ms to ~1.1s in our tests, caveat: your model size and quantization matter.
00:01:58 - Alex Kim: hmm that matches some of our telemetry. we're also interested in batching — we do both synchronous inference and async batch jobs — how should we set targeting batch sizes?
00:02:10 - Priya Shah: batching is workload dependent; tiny batches keep latency low but lower throughput; larger batches improve throughput but increase tail. Redwood's smart-batcher does dynamic batching based on request SLOs; you can set max wait window (e.g. 5-25ms) to balance. In Dedicated you can increase concurrency with more GPUs to keep batch sizes small while maintaining throughput.
00:02:35 - Jordan Price: any empirical numbers for p95/p99 with batching on T4 vs A100?
00:02:43 - Priya Shah: yes ballpark — for a 13B model on A100, with small batches and kv cache warm, p95 might be ~90-120ms and p99 ~190-250ms; on T4 p95 ~180-300ms and p99 ~350-600ms. again depends on token length and quantization.
00:03:00 - Alex Kim: okay, and streaming? we're doing teleop so per-token latency matters.
00:03:08 - Priya Shah: streaming reduces perceived latency by delivering partial tokens; however end-to-end p99 for final token can still be affected by tails. Important patterns: (1) enable prefix caching to avoid recomputing context, (2) use smaller kv shards to reduce lock contention, (3) keep network hops low. For token-by-token, A100 with NVLink-attached instances and local peering gives best results.
00:03:35 - Rita Chen: security question — if we go Private (VPC) or on-prem, how do you handle KMS and audit logs?
00:03:44 - Sam Turner: good question, Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS, HSM integrations, and we ship audit logs to your S3 or SIEM; we'll send SOC2 and encryption docs after the call.
00:03:58 - Maya Lopez: Priya, you said kv cache shards — can you expand on eviction and consistency across replicas?
00:04:06 - Priya Shah: sure, we do sharded kv cache with per-replica LRU and synchronous invalidation on model updates; warm caches are per-replica so we do cross-replica prewarm during canary rollouts. If you have strict consistency needs we can configure sticky routing to pinned workers. That reduces cold cache misses but can hurt load balance.
00:04:30 - Jordan Price: what's the impact of quantization on latency vs quality? we were considering 4-bit quant for cost savings.
00:04:39 - Priya Shah: quantization generally improves latency and memory footprint—int4 gives big speedups especially on newer kernels optimized for 4-bit. On some models you may see minor quality regression on edge cases; our Optimize tooling can recommend quant profile per workload. Operationally, quantized models reduce p95/p99 because they cut kernel time and allow more effective batching.
00:05:00 - Alex Kim: any gotchas for on-prem network hops? we have a multi-datacenter setup and worried about inter-dc hops.
00:05:08 - Diego Ramos: Diego here — we usually see inter-dc hops add jitter from 2-20ms depending on backbone. For p99 this compounds when combined with retries or large KV fetches. Recommendation: keep inference path inside a single AZ where possible and use async replication for model updates.
00:05:28 - Priya Shah: also worth instrumenting distributed traces end-to-end; we attach a trace id and you can see token-level spans — network wait, kernel compute, kv lookup. That helps narrow whether a tail is network or compute.
00:05:44 - Maya Lopez: can you explain streaming vs non-streaming in terms of SLO calculations?
00:05:50 - Priya Shah: for streaming you need two SLOs: first-byte latency (time to first emitted token) and final-token latency; many customers set first-byte p95 tight (e.g., 150ms) and allow a looser final-token p99. For non-streaming you only have final response which often bumps p99 so it's harder for interactive use.
00:06:10 - Alex Kim: do you support on-the-fly fallback to smaller models when p99 exceeds threshold?
00:06:16 - Priya Shah: yes, smart routing can failover to lighter quantized variants or smaller models; you can configure deterministic fallback paths or probabilistic sampling for quality checks. Keep in mind fallbacks can change semantics so include canary checks.
00:06:30 - Jordan Price: any instrumentation you recommend to separate network tail vs kernel tail?
00:06:36 - Priya Shah: collect distributed traces with spans for: client->loadbalancer, lb->worker, worker compute start/end, kv lookup, and downstream storage. Network tails look like long client->lb or lb->worker spans; kernel tails are compute spans with long durations.
00:06:52 - Rita Chen: on compliance, what about data residency for telemetry? we need logs to stay in EU for some workloads.
00:07:00 - Sam Turner: we support region-restricted storage for logs and metrics in Private; for Hosted we offer EU region deployments with data residency controls. We'll include that in the security packet.
00:07:12 - Alex Kim: great, can we go over the benchmark plan? what do you need from us?
00:07:18 - Priya Shah: we'll run a 2-hour benchmark with: representative prompt distribution, token length histogram, concurrency profile, and both streaming/non-streaming runs; we'll toggle kv cache warm/cold and run quantized vs full-precision. We'll instrument p50/p95/p99 and provide raw traces.
00:07:38 - Maya Lopez: we'll upload payloads and share S3 link by Monday.
00:07:42 - Sam Turner: perfect. last, pricing and Dedicated sizing: we'll send a draft recommendation for Dedicated GPU counts and expected cost vs hosted.
00:07:52 - Alex Kim: thanks, this was helpful, a few quick clarifying q's — when you say warm-cache prewarm, what's the prewarm time and cost?
00:08:00 - Priya Shah: prewarm depends on corpus size; for typical session histories we prewarm in minutes with lightweight synthetic requests; cost is minimal compared to serving. We'll include numbers in the spreadsheet.
00:08:14 - Jordan Price: one more — if we do VPC peering, any port or MTU considerations?
00:08:19 - Diego Ramos: ensure MTU consistency across path, keep idle TCP timeouts aligned to prevent unexpected socket resets, and allow ports for healthcheck/metrics. Details in infra doc we'll send.
00:08:33 - Sam Turner: awesome, thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the benchmark plan and security docs.
00:08:40 - Alex Kim: sounds good, thanks all.
00:08:42 - (meeting ends)
